title: Shemini: the eighth day (Leviticus 9:1)
hook: after seven days of preparation, the service begins on the eighth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the new priests stood seven days in the doorway of the tent. Your line was wait at the door. What did you pause before? Today, a new portion, and the waiting ends. Day three hundred ninety.

Seven is the number of a complete week. Six days of work, one of rest, and then it starts over. Shabbat keeps that loop turning. So what's an eighth day? In Jewish life, it keeps showing up at the moments when something new begins. A baby boy is brought into the covenant on his eighth day. The festival of Sukkot is followed by an eighth day of its own. And this week's portion is named for it. Shemini. Eighth. After a week of waiting at the door, the priests finally step through.
screen: `SEVEN: A COMPLETE WEEK.` → `THE EIGHTH DAY KEEPS SHOWING UP.` → `SHEMINI: EIGHTH.`

segments.voice: In the JPS 1917 translation: "And it came to pass on the eighth day, that Moses called Aaron and his sons, and the elders of Israel." The rabbis say this was the first day of the first month, Nisan, the very day the sanctuary was set up for good. The Talmud says that day took ten crowns: it was the first of many things, the first day the priests served, the first day the people's offerings were brought there, the first day God's presence rested among them. Moses tells Aaron what to bring, and adds the reason: for today the LORD appears to you. Then Aaron, who has watched for seven days, does it himself for the first time. The offering for himself, the offering for the people. And when it's done, the Torah says, Aaron lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them. Rashi says this was the priestly blessing, the one still said in synagogues today: may the Lord bless you and keep you. Then Moses and Aaron go into the tent together, come out, and bless the people again. The glory of the Lord appears to everyone. Fire comes out and consumes the offering on the altar, and the people see it, shout for joy and fall on their faces. Why does so much begin on an eighth day? Some teachers say seven is the natural world, complete in itself, and eight is one step beyond it: the place where the holy breaks in. The week of preparation was full. The eighth day is when it begins.
screen: `THE FIRST OF NISAN: TEN CROWNS.` · `TODAY THE LORD APPEARS TO YOU.` · `AARON LIFTS HIS HANDS AND BLESSES.` · `SEVEN IS NATURE; EIGHT IS BEYOND.` · then, large: `THE EIGHTH DAY BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin something you've prepared for. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been getting ready for: a project you've researched, a call you've rehearsed, a habit you've planned, a book you bought and never opened. You've had your seven days. Now the eighth: the first real step, today, not perfectly, just actually. Notice what it's like to stop preparing and start. Breathe in on the preparing, breathe out on the beginning. The bell holds the time.
Shemini. Eighth. The portion that opens on the eighth day, when the priests' preparation ends and their service begins.
Your line: the eighth day begins. Today, take the first real step on something you've been preparing for. Day three hundred ninety.

howItsDone: The priestly blessing that tradition links to Aaron's first blessing on the eighth day is still recited in synagogues by kohanim, descendants of Aaron, with hands raised toward the congregation.

what it means: the day preparation ends and the priests' service, and God's presence among the people, begins.

what a scholar hears: Shabbat 87b says the day took ten crowns; Rashi on 9:22 identifies Aaron's blessing as birkat kohanim; the eighth day as beyond nature is a theme in later thought, e.g., the Maharal.
